First of Many.

I've spent the last year and a half building AI-native products at a venture studio — across healthcare, consumer, internal tooling, and more. Different industries, same question every time:

What does the workflow look like when AI isn't bolted on, but built in from day one?

Right now, the default play is finding a bottleneck and dropping an AI tool into it. Summarize this. Automate that. And that works — but it's the tip of the iceberg.

The bigger opportunity isn't inserting AI into existing processes. It's rethinking the processes entirely. The workflows we operate in were designed before intelligent automation existed — built around human constraints that are changing fast. The workflows should too.

And the people best positioned to see this? Not the founders on your timeline. It's the people in the trenches — the ones who operate inside these systems every day and know exactly where things break. The difference now is that the tools exist to actually build something about it.

That's what we do at Conduit Venture Labs. Real problems, real industries, AI-native products from scratch. I've been the principal engineer driving that work across multiple domains — and I'm going to start sharing it publicly. The builds, the architecture, the business thinking, and the lessons.
This is the first of many. 

If you're building in this space — or thinking about it — follow along.

The Toronto Machine Learning Summit 2025

2 weeks ago, I had the opportunity to listen and speak with a lot of people doing cool things. Working at a venture studio means I’m dialled-in 24/7, and my main source of tech news is TLDR or a message from Amish Patel about a new tool to try out; so it was great to actually get out and hear what everyone else is doing.

The summit itself was nice overall. Definitely gained a lot of perspective (both validating and critical) about my general outlook on building with and for AI.

1. Build with resource modularity in mind. Assume that chat completion, embedding, and semantic models are going to improve over time. We should be able to hotswap the “next best” easily.

2. Orchestration is trending. Single powerhouse agents/systems are being pushed aside for collections of autonomous tools that integrate well together.

3. AI Foresight will win. Diederik van Liere dropped the most impactful bar of the summit: “people overestimate the short term impact of AI, and underestimate the long-term impact”. I know what this means to me, interested in hearing other perspectives.

Ended up talking with a bunch of people there and honestly, I think tech is in a good spot. Builders and innovators are learning how to process a waterfall of new information and integrate cutting edge tools into their stacks while the enterprise begins the shift to AI-native systems.

Looking forward to my next conference!

There’s so much value in being a technical generalist. Having a knack for problem solving (domain specific or generalized), a “go for it” outlook, and industry-relevant knowledge (whether you’ve known about it for years or can read up on it) will make you stand out.

0-1 looks different for everyone. Having multiple assets to leverage will give you the confidence to push hard - especially in the hectic job market of today.

@ all the engineers and CS ppl - there is no discrete “career” path/paths. Make your own.

Getting ghosted was the best thing to happen to me.

I sent out about a hundred applications and a dozen emails post grad, trying to land a job. I even reached out to old bosses and colleagues - and didn’t hear back. 

Until it all fell into place.

Here’s what I learned:

1. At the end of the day, you need to leverage your network. Everyone has a rockstar resume - it’s pretty hard to not have one. Having a foot in the door when you apply to a job isn’t a handout - it’s a product of a relationship you created, and definitely something you earned. Don’t be too prideful in how you get your starts.

2. Expand your search.

a) So many new SWE and CS grads struggle getting a job right after school… LinkedIn/glassdor/google is not the end all be all for job searches. It’s important to be aware of the businesses in your city. Door knock, email, whatever, just put yourself out there.

b) Look for roles outside the traditional ‘X-ware developer/engineer/analyst/scientist’. There’s a ton of room for enthusiastic, entry level ppl in the niche market.

3. YOLO. Rejection literally doesn’t matter. Start your own business, learn, just do something. It’ll all work out. Be resilient (start with being delusional if you need to lol)

You can’t control whether someone wants to take a chance with you, but if they do, make that the best decision they ever made.
